passage: Note for Payal's parents, Tuesday. At snack time a steel tray slid off the counter and crashed. Payal went stiff, eyes wide, then wailed and crawled straight into my lap. I held her and said, "Big bang. The tray fell. You're safe." She peeked at the tray, sniffed, and after a few minutes went back to her banana. From tomorrow I'll tell the children before we move the noisy trays. Maria 🙂

qa.q: What fell and crashed at snack time?
qa.a: A steel tray slid off the counter and crashed at snack time.

qa.q: What does Payal going stiff and crawling into Maria's lap suggest she felt?
qa.a: It suggests the sudden crash frightened her, and she went to Maria because she wanted to feel safe again.

qa.q: Which of Maria's choices helped Payal settle, and why?
qa.a: Holding Payal and naming the noise in simple words helped her calm down, and warning the children before moving trays can stop the shock from happening again.

qa.q: How might Payal's parents feel reading this note?
qa.a: They may feel reassured that Maria noticed Payal's fright and comforted her quickly. 😊

grounding: Shows a toddler's instinctive fear reaction to a sudden loud noise and a calm adult comforting her.

passage: The village fair was busy with bangle stalls and swings. Irawati rode on her Aaba Shankar's shoulders, clapping at the colours. Then a drummer beside the temple steps started beating hard without warning. Irawati jerked, grabbed two fistfuls of Shankar's hair and let out a thin cry. Shankar lifted her down and held her against his chest, walking to the quiet side of the pond. She kept her face hidden for a while, then slowly turned to watch the drummer from far away.

qa.q: Where did Shankar carry Irawati after the drumming started?
qa.a: He carried her to the quiet side of the pond.

qa.q: Why did Irawati grab Shankar's hair and cry out?
qa.a: The drumming began suddenly and loudly, so she was startled and scared, and she held on to the person she felt safest with.

qa.q: What did Shankar do that suited a frightened toddler?
qa.a: He moved her away from the noise and held her close without hurrying her, letting her look again only when she was ready.

qa.q: What would change if Shankar had stayed near the drummer and told her not to cry?
qa.a: Irawati would likely have stayed frightened and cried harder, because the loud sound would keep hitting her and her fear would not be comforted.

grounding: Illustrates a toddler's instinctive fear of a sudden loud noise in a crowded, unfamiliar place.

passage: On a windy Saturday in a park in Cape Town, Daniel toddled after a rolling ball while his father Thabo sat on the grass. A large brown dog came bounding out from behind a bench. Daniel stopped dead, threw his arms up and screamed, then ran back and clung to Thabo's leg. Thabo scooped him up and asked the owner to call the dog. From his father's arms, Daniel watched the dog sit, his fingers still gripping Thabo's shirt.

qa.q: What came out from behind the bench?
qa.a: A large brown dog came bounding out from behind a bench.

qa.q: What does Daniel's grip on Thabo's shirt show about how he felt, even after the dog sat?
qa.a: It shows he still felt uneasy and wanted to stay close to his father, because the dog had appeared so suddenly.

qa.q: How could Thabo help Daniel feel calmer around dogs over time?
qa.a: He could let Daniel watch calm dogs from a safe distance in his arms, and never push him to touch one before he is ready.

qa.q: How might the dog's owner see Daniel's scream?
qa.a: The owner might think the dog was only being playful, but could also understand that a big dog rushing up is scary for a small child.

grounding: Shows a toddler's instinctive fear reaction to a sudden movement by a large dog.

passage: I'm Lavanya from the flat next door. I was visiting when Irfan's Ammi held out a spoon of mashed bitter gourd. Irfan, not yet two, pressed his lips shut and twisted his head away. A little got in anyway; he scrunched his nose, pushed it out with his tongue and shoved the bowl. Later, wet sand stuck to his palms at the park, and he held his hands out stiffly, whining, until they were wiped. I can't know what he thought, but he clearly wanted neither.

qa.q: What food did Irfan's Ammi offer him?
qa.a: She offered him a spoon of mashed bitter gourd.

qa.q: What did Irfan's scrunched nose and stiff hands suggest about how he felt?
qa.a: They suggest he found the bitter taste and the wet, sticky sand unpleasant and wanted them gone.

qa.q: What small step could help Irfan get used to bitter gourd?
qa.a: His Ammi could put a tiny piece beside food he likes and let him touch or taste it without pressure, offering it again on other days.

qa.q: Why is Lavanya careful to say they can't know what Irfan thought?
qa.a: Lavanya is only watching from outside, so Lavanya can see his face and actions but can only guess at what was going on inside him.

grounding: Illustrates a toddler rejecting an unfamiliar bitter taste and an unpleasant texture, seen by a neighbour.

passage:
Monday: Gautam put a spoon of plain curd near Nikita's lips. She gagged, spat it onto her bib and pushed his hand away.
Thursday: He left a small dab of curd at the edge of her plate beside the rice she loves. She poked it, licked her finger, grimaced, and went back to the rice.
The next Sunday: She dipped a rice ball into the curd herself, made a face at the first bite, then ate two more.

qa.q: What did Gautam put beside Nikita's rice on Thursday?
qa.a: He left a small dab of curd at the edge of her plate beside the rice.

qa.q: What does Nikita's gag on Monday show about how the curd felt to her?
qa.a: It shows the sour taste and cold texture were strange and unpleasant to her, so she rejected it straight away.

qa.q: Why did Gautam's slow approach work better than insisting on Monday?
qa.a: Leaving a little curd nearby let Nikita explore it at her own pace, next to food she already trusted, so the new taste became less of a shock. 👍

qa.q: How might Gautam have felt on Sunday watching her eat it?
qa.a: He might have felt pleased and relieved that his patience paid off, even though she still pulled a face at first.

grounding: Shows a toddler rejecting an unfamiliar taste and slowly accepting it over several days.

passage: The first cold morning in their Delhi flat, Sumit pulled a new woollen sweater over his son Naveen's head. Within seconds Naveen was squirming, tugging at the neck and whimpering. He scratched his arms, arched his back and finally flopped on the floor, crying and yanking the sleeves. Sumit knelt and ran his hand over the wool; it felt scratchy. He took it off, slipped a soft cotton vest on first, and put the sweater back over it. Naveen sniffed and toddled off to his blocks.

qa.q: What did Sumit put on Naveen under the sweater?
qa.a: He slipped a soft cotton vest on first and put the sweater back over it.

qa.q: Why was Naveen tugging and crying in the new sweater?
qa.a: The wool felt scratchy against his skin, and that uncomfortable feeling upset him enough that he wanted it off.

qa.q: What did Sumit do that a parent could copy?
qa.a: He checked the sweater himself to find the cause and changed the layer instead of scolding Naveen for fussing.

qa.q: What would change if Sumit had assumed Naveen was just being naughty?
qa.a: Naveen would probably keep crying and fighting the sweater, and the morning would turn into a struggle over something that really bothered him.

grounding: Illustrates a toddler rejecting an unpleasant sensory input, a scratchy fabric.

passage:
Friday: At the neighbour's birthday party, Gurleen's red balloon slipped from her fist and floated over the rooftops. She stretched both arms up, wailed and wouldn't be held by anyone but her mother, Nikita.
Saturday: She pointed at the empty sky from the balcony. "Gone," she said, lower lip trembling. Nikita hugged her and said, "Yes, gone. You miss it."
Tuesday: Seeing balloons at a shop, Gurleen went quiet, then took Nikita's hand and walked on.

qa.q: What happened to Gurleen's balloon at the party?
qa.a: Her red balloon slipped from her fist and floated over the rooftops.

qa.q: What does Gurleen's trembling lip on Saturday suggest?
qa.a: It suggests she was still sad about losing the balloon and missed it, even a day later.

qa.q: How did Nikita's words help Gurleen with her loss?
qa.a: By saying "Yes, gone. You miss it," Nikita put simple words to Gurleen's sadness instead of rushing to distract her, which helped her feel understood. 🤍

qa.q: What might it be like for Nikita to watch Gurleen go quiet near the balloon shop?
qa.a: She might feel a small tug of sympathy, but also relief that Gurleen could notice the balloons and still walk on holding her hand.

grounding: Shows a toddler expressing unhappiness over losing a desired object and slowly coming to terms with it.

passage: The metro was packed at six in the evening. Lavanya, fourteen months old, was teething, and her cheeks were red. She rubbed her face against her mother Rashmi's shoulder, then arched back and wailed, drool soaking her collar. Passengers turned to look. Rashmi swayed gently, pulled a cool teether from her bag and let Lavanya gnaw on it, humming close to her ear. The crying faded to hiccupping sobs, and by the next stop Lavanya was clutching the teether, eyes half shut.

qa.q: Where were Lavanya and Rashmi at six in the evening?
qa.a: They were in a packed metro at six in the evening.

qa.q: Why did Lavanya rub her face and wail?
qa.a: Her teething gums were sore, and being tired in a crowded train likely made the discomfort feel worse.

qa.q: What helped Lavanya's crying fade?
qa.a: Rashmi swaying, humming close to her ear and giving her a cool teether to gnaw eased both the soreness and the upset.

qa.q: How might other passengers see Rashmi in that moment?
qa.a: Some might be annoyed by the noise, but many would see a mother calmly doing her best with an uncomfortable baby in a hard place.

grounding: Illustrates a toddler expressing discomfort through crying and a caregiver soothing it.

passage:
"Broke!" Sabina held up two halves of her red crayon, her chin wobbling.
"Oh no, it snapped," said her big sister Rashmi, putting down her schoolbook.
"Broke! Red broke!" Sabina threw the pieces and began to sob.
"You're sad. Red was your favourite."
"Mine red!"
"Come here." Rashmi pulled her onto her lap. "Look, both pieces still colour. One for you, one for me?"
Sabina sniffed, took the longer piece and scribbled a wobbly sun on Rashmi's notebook.

qa.q: What did Sabina draw at the end?
qa.a: She scribbled a wobbly sun on Rashmi's notebook.

qa.q: How can you tell Sabina felt upset about the crayon?
qa.a: Her chin wobbled, she threw the pieces and sobbed, and she kept insisting "Mine red!" because her favourite crayon was broken.

qa.q: Which of Rashmi's moves helped most, and why?
qa.a: Naming the feeling first and then showing that both halves still colour helped, because Sabina felt heard before being offered a way forward.

qa.q: What would change if Rashmi had said, "It's just a crayon, stop crying"?
qa.a: Sabina would likely feel dismissed and cry longer, since the loss felt big to her even if it looked small to an older child.

grounding: Shows a toddler expressing unhappiness at the loss of a desired object, a favourite crayon.

passage:
Sunday: Deepika hid her face behind a dupatta. When she whipped it away, Pankaj's eyes went round and his mouth fell open; then he shrieked with laughter and slapped the mattress for more.
Wednesday: The lid of his new toy box popped up on a spring. Pankaj jumped, stared, and then pushed it shut to make it pop again.
Next Monday: He crouched behind the curtain, waited, and burst out at Deepika, squealing, "Boo!"

qa.q: What did Deepika hide her face behind on Sunday?
qa.a: She hid her face behind a dupatta.

qa.q: What do Pankaj's round eyes and open mouth suggest when the dupatta came away?
qa.a: They suggest a moment of real surprise before he realised it was a game, which is why the shock turned into laughter.

qa.q: How could Deepika keep building on Pankaj's love of surprises?
qa.a: She could keep playing simple hide-and-reveal games with him and let him take turns being the one who surprises her. 🎉

qa.q: How might Deepika feel when Pankaj bursts out at her from the curtain?
qa.a: She would likely be delighted, since he is now creating the surprise himself instead of only reacting to it.

grounding: Shows a toddler reacting to unexpected events such as peek-a-boo and a pop-up lid, then playing with surprise.

passage: In their Chennai flat, Deepak was stacking cups on the floor when the power went off. The fan slowed, the room went dim, and he froze with a cup in his hand, staring at his Ammamma, Keerthana. A minute later the lights snapped back and the fan whirred. Deepak gasped, pointed up and shouted, "Light!" Keerthana gasped too, copying him, and he laughed so hard he sat down with a bump.

qa.q: What was Deepak doing when the power went off?
qa.a: He was stacking cups on the floor.

qa.q: Why did Deepak freeze and stare at Keerthana when the room went dim?
qa.a: The sudden change caught him off guard, and he seemed to look to her to see whether it was something to worry about.

qa.q: What did Keerthana's copied gasp do for Deepak?
qa.a: It shared his surprise and turned it into a game, showing him the change was safe and even funny. 😊

qa.q: What would change if Keerthana had looked frightened during the power cut?
qa.a: Deepak might have read her face as a sign of danger and started crying instead of laughing.

grounding: Illustrates a toddler reacting to a sudden change in his surroundings.

passage:
"Ready?" Vinita dipped the wand and blew. A cloud of bubbles drifted over the balcony.
Darshan reached out. One popped right on his nose. He blinked hard and went still.
"Oh! It popped on you!" said Vinita.
"Pop!" Darshan touched his nose, then looked at her, wide-eyed.
"Pop," she agreed, smiling.
"Again! Again!"
"Here comes another one."
This time he squeezed his eyes shut and giggled before it even landed.

qa.q: Where did one of the bubbles pop?
qa.a: One bubble popped right on Darshan's nose.

qa.q: What does Darshan's blinking and going still tell you about how he felt?
qa.a: It shows he was startled by the unexpected pop and needed a moment to work out what had happened.

qa.q: How did Vinita help turn Darshan's startle into fun?
qa.a: She named what happened in a cheerful voice and agreed with his word "Pop", so he felt safe enough to ask for more.

qa.q: Why might Darshan react differently the second time?
qa.a: He now expected the pop, so instead of being caught off guard he giggled in anticipation before it landed.

grounding: Shows a toddler's surprise at an unexpected event and how it turns into playful anticipation.

passage: In the colony park in Ludhiana, Gurleen climbed the low slide while her mother Minakshi sat on the bench. Halfway up, Gurleen looked back. Minakshi waved. Gurleen slid down, tripped on the grass and scraped her palm. She ran straight to the bench, holding her hand out. Minakshi blew on it and held her until the crying stopped. Then Gurleen slipped off her lap and ran back to the slide, glancing once at the bench.

qa.q: Where was Minakshi sitting while Gurleen played?
qa.a: Minakshi sat on the bench in the colony park.

qa.q: Why did Gurleen look back at the bench halfway up the slide?
qa.a: She wanted to check that her mother was still there, and seeing Minakshi wave made her feel safe to keep going.

qa.q: How does Minakshi's steady presence support Gurleen's play?
qa.a: Because Minakshi stays in view and comforts her quickly when she is hurt, Gurleen feels secure enough to go back and explore on her own.

qa.q: What would change if Minakshi often walked away without Gurleen knowing?
qa.a: Gurleen might stop exploring and cling instead, because she could no longer count on her mother being there when she needed her.

grounding: Shows a toddler's trust that her caregiver will be there to meet her needs, which lets her explore.

passage:
"Mama?" Varun's voice came from the cot in the dark.
"I'm here, jaan," said Salma, turning on the small lamp.
"Milk."
"Milk is coming. Let me warm it."
Varun sat up, holding the cot bars, and watched the door. He didn't cry.
"Here it is." She sat on the floor beside him while he drank.
"Mama stay."
"I'll stay till you're sleepy."
He handed back the cup, lay down and curled his fingers round her thumb.

qa.q: What did Varun ask for when he woke?
qa.a: He asked for milk.

qa.q: Why didn't Varun cry while waiting for the milk?
qa.a: He seems sure from experience that when Salma says milk is coming, it really will come, so he can wait calmly.

qa.q: What in Salma's replies builds Varun's sense of security?
qa.a: She answers him right away, tells him exactly what will happen and then does it, so her words and actions match.

qa.q: What might Salma feel as Varun curls his fingers round her thumb?
qa.a: She would likely feel tired but tender, knowing her steady care is what lets him settle back to sleep. ❤️

grounding: Illustrates a toddler's secure trust that his caregiver will meet his physical and emotional needs.

passage:
Monthly note on Payal, from Asif at the day-care.
When Payal joined in June, she screamed at drop-off and wouldn't let me hold her. I kept to the same steps every day: greet her at the gate, offer her the blue cushion, snack after circle time.
By now she waves bye to her father and toddles in. When she's hungry, she comes and taps the snack shelf, then waits. Yesterday she fell asleep on my arm during story. 😊

qa.q: What did Payal do at drop-off when she first joined in June?
qa.a: She screamed at drop-off and wouldn't let Asif hold her.

qa.q: What does Payal tapping the snack shelf and then waiting suggest she believes?
qa.a: It suggests she now believes Asif will notice and give her food, so she trusts her need will be met without crying.

qa.q: Which of Asif's habits helped Payal settle in?
qa.a: Doing the same steps every day, from greeting her at the gate to snack after circle time, made the day predictable and let her trust Asif.

qa.q: How might Payal's father feel reading this note?
qa.a: He would likely feel relieved and grateful that she has gone from screaming at drop-off to waving bye and resting on Asif's arm. 🙏

grounding: Shows a toddler building secure trust that a consistent caregiver will meet her needs.

passage: Every evening I, Ramesh, water the plants on my balcony across the lane, and I see little Trisha at her gate. When her Nani comes back from the vegetable market, Trisha runs with her arms up, pats Nani's cheeks with both hands and presses her face into her sari. Yesterday I offered Trisha a biscuit over the wall. She took it, smiled shyly, then trotted back and climbed into Nani's lap to eat it.

qa.q: Where does Ramesh water the plants?
qa.a: Ramesh waters them on the balcony across the lane.

qa.q: What does Trisha running with her arms up suggest about her feelings for Nani?
qa.a: It suggests she is happy and excited to see Nani and feels strong love and closeness towards her.

qa.q: How could Nani respond to keep that warmth growing?
qa.a: She could bend down to meet Trisha's hug, talk to her warmly and give her a little unhurried time when she gets home.

qa.q: How might Ramesh feel when Trisha takes the biscuit but goes back to Nani?
qa.a: Ramesh is probably not hurt, and may feel amused and touched to see how clearly Trisha prefers her Nani.

grounding: Illustrates a toddler showing warmth and a clear preference for her primary caregiver, seen by a neighbour.

passage:
Day one: Deepak came home after three weeks at a work site. Rashmi hid behind Dadi's knees and only stared at her Papa.
Day two: She walked over with her stuffed rabbit, dropped it in his lap, and sat close enough to touch his arm.
Day four: When the doorbell rang in the evening, she ran shouting, "Papa!", hugged his legs and planted a wet kiss on his cheek when he lifted her.

qa.q: How long had Deepak been away at the work site?
qa.a: He had been away for three weeks at a work site.

qa.q: Why might Rashmi have hidden behind Dadi on the first day?
qa.a: After three weeks apart she may have felt shy and unsure, needing time to feel close to her Papa again.

qa.q: What could Deepak do to help the closeness return?
qa.a: He could stay calm and warm, let Rashmi come to him in her own time and accept small gifts like the rabbit with delight.

qa.q: What is it like for Deepak when Rashmi runs to the door on day four?
qa.a: It likely feels wonderful after the shy first day, showing him their bond is back. ❤️

grounding: Shows a toddler's warmth and preference for a primary caregiver returning over a few days.

passage: At a family engagement in a busy Hyderabad hall, two-year-old Aditi was passed from aunt to aunt. Each time, she twisted round to find her Ammi, Sabina, and stretched out her arms. When she was finally handed back, she sighed, laid her head on Sabina's shoulder and patted her cheek. Later she broke off a sticky bit of her laddoo and pushed it into Sabina's mouth, watching her face until she chewed.

qa.q: Where was the engagement held?
qa.a: It was held in a busy Hyderabad hall.

qa.q: What does Aditi sighing on Sabina's shoulder suggest?
qa.a: It suggests she felt relieved and comforted to be back with her Ammi after being passed around.

qa.q: How could relatives respect Aditi's wish to be with Sabina?
qa.a: They could greet her while she stays on Sabina's lap and let her come to them when she wants, instead of passing her around.

qa.q: How might Sabina feel when Aditi feeds her the laddoo?
qa.a: She would likely feel touched by this small, sticky act of love and sharing.

grounding: Illustrates a toddler showing love and preference for her primary caregiver among many relatives.

passage:
"Ammi, no go!" Sunaina wrapped both arms round Zeenat's leg at Nani's door.
"I'm going to work, and I'll come back after your nap," said Zeenat, kneeling.
"No! No go!" Sunaina's face crumpled and she sobbed, clinging tighter.
"Here, keep my scarf. It smells like me."
Nani held out her arms. "Come, your cup is ready."
Zeenat kissed her, said, "Bye, see you after nap," and left.
Sunaina wailed at the window, the scarf pressed to her cheek.

qa.q: What did Zeenat give Sunaina before leaving?
qa.a: She gave Sunaina her scarf, saying it smells like her.

qa.q: Why did Sunaina cling to Zeenat's leg and sob?
qa.a: She was scared and upset at being parted from her Ammi, the person who makes her feel safest.

qa.q: Which parts of Zeenat's goodbye were helpful?
qa.a: She told Sunaina simply when she would return, left something comforting and said a clear goodbye instead of sneaking away.

qa.q: What might this goodbye be like for Nani?
qa.a: It may be hard to hear Sunaina wail, but Nani can stay close and comfort her until the crying eases. 🤍

grounding: Shows a toddler's distress at being separated from her main attachment figure.

passage:
Playgroup note on Farhan, Monday, from Rehana.
When his Abbu left this morning, Farhan stood at the door calling "Abbu! Abbu!" and pushed away every toy I offered. I sat on the floor near him, not too close, and said, "Abbu will come after lunch." After a long while he let me hold his hand and we filled cups at the water table. When Abbu came back, Farhan ran and clung to his neck. Tomorrow I'll suggest one short, same goodbye each day.

qa.q: What did Farhan do when his Abbu left?
qa.a: He stood at the door calling "Abbu! Abbu!" and pushed away every toy Rehana offered.

qa.q: What does Farhan clinging to his Abbu's neck at pickup suggest?
qa.a: It suggests he had felt anxious all morning and felt huge relief to have his Abbu back.

qa.q: Why is Rehana's idea of a short, same goodbye each day a good one?
qa.a: A predictable goodbye helps Farhan learn that Abbu always leaves and always comes back, which can slowly ease his distress.

qa.q: How might Farhan's Abbu feel leaving him crying at the door?
qa.a: He might feel guilty and worried, and Rehana's note could reassure him that Farhan was comforted and did settle.

grounding: Illustrates a toddler's separation distress at playgroup and a caregiver's gentle support.

passage: Early on market day in the kasba, Asif climbed onto the local bus with sacks of onions to sell in town. From the gate, Parul saw him go. She strained against her Dadi's arms, screaming, one hand stretched toward the bus as it rattled away. For a long time she stood by the gate, sniffling and refusing her roti. At dusk the bus horn sounded. Parul ran barefoot to the gate and would not let go of her Abbu's kurta all evening.

qa.q: What did Asif take to sell in town?
qa.a: He took sacks of onions to sell in town.

qa.q: What does Parul refusing her roti suggest about how she felt?
qa.a: It suggests she was still upset and worried after her Abbu left, too distressed to think about food.

qa.q: How could Asif make market-day partings easier for Parul?
qa.a: He could say a short, warm goodbye before leaving and tell her he will come back with the evening bus, so she knows what to expect.

qa.q: What is it like for Dadi when Parul strains and screams in her arms?
qa.a: It is probably tiring and sad for her, though she can keep comforting Parul and keep her safe until Asif returns.

grounding: Shows a toddler's separation anxiety when parted from her father in a small-town setting.

passage:
Monday: Maria was hanging clothes on the balcony in Goa when a peg dropped. Gargi toddled over, picked it up and held it high until Maria took it.
Wednesday: Maria came in with shopping bags in both hands. Gargi ran and pushed the half-closed door wide open, then went back to her blocks.
Saturday: Maria's spoon clattered off the table. Before anyone spoke, Gargi fetched it and handed it up, not waiting for a thank-you.

qa.q: What did Gargi do on Wednesday when Maria came in with shopping bags?
qa.a: She ran and pushed the half-closed door wide open, then went back to her blocks.

qa.q: Why do you think Gargi picks things up without being asked?
qa.a: She seems to notice when Maria needs something and simply wants to help, not to earn a reward.

qa.q: How can Maria encourage Gargi's helping without turning it into a reward game?
qa.a: She can warmly say what Gargi did, like "You opened the door for me," rather than offering sweets for each help.

qa.q: What would change if Maria only praised Gargi when she had asked her to help?
qa.a: Gargi might start helping only on request, and her natural, unasked kindness could fade.

grounding: Shows a toddler spontaneously picking up dropped items and helping without prompt or reward over several days.

passage: In their Bengaluru flat, Lakshmi Paati bent over the newspaper and her glasses slid off and skittered under the sofa. She sighed and began to lower herself to her knees. Nitin, two, dropped his toy truck, crawled flat under the sofa and came out holding the glasses by one arm. He pushed them into her hand. When her pen rolled off the table a moment later, he grabbed that too, then went straight back to his truck.

qa.q: Where did Lakshmi Paati's glasses slide?
qa.a: Her glasses slid off and skittered under the sofa.

qa.q: What might Nitin have noticed that made him drop his truck?
qa.a: He probably saw Paati sigh and start to kneel, and seemed to understand she needed help reaching the glasses.

qa.q: How could Lakshmi Paati respond to Nitin's help?
qa.a: She could thank him simply and warmly so he knows his help mattered, without making a fuss or offering a treat.

qa.q: How might Lakshmi Paati see Nitin crawling under the sofa for her?
qa.a: She would likely feel grateful and touched that such a small child noticed her struggle and helped on his own. 😊

grounding: Illustrates a toddler spontaneously fetching dropped items for an elder without being asked.

passage:
"Oops, my keys!" Sunaina said as they hit the floor by the door.
Uday, who was pulling on one sandal, dropped it and waddled over. "Keys!"
"Oh, you got them?"
"Here, Mummy." He held them up with both hands.
"Thank you, Uday."
He was already back at his sandal. A minute later her dupatta slipped off her shoulder. Uday tugged the end and lifted it up to her.
"Look at you, noticing everything," she laughed.

qa.q: What was Uday doing when the keys fell?
qa.a: He was pulling on one sandal by the door.

qa.q: What does Uday going straight back to his sandal suggest about why he helped?
qa.a: It suggests he helped because he wanted to, not for praise or a reward, since he didn't wait around for more.

qa.q: What could Sunaina say next time to encourage this kind of help?
qa.a: She could name exactly what he did, such as "You picked up my keys," so he sees how his help made a difference.

qa.q: How might Sunaina feel when Uday lifts her dupatta up to her?
qa.a: She would probably feel amused and warm, surprised at how quickly he notices small things she needs.

grounding: Shows a toddler spontaneously picking up dropped items for his mother without prompt or reward.

passage: I'm Leela, Harsha's cousin, and I stayed at their house during the holidays. Before dinner, Harsha dragged his little stool to the sink on his own, rubbed the soap into bubbles and held his wet hands up for the towel, grinning. But at bedtime, when his mother brought his pyjamas, he threw himself on the floor, kicking and yelling "No!" I couldn't tell if he was tired or just wanted to keep playing. Maybe both.

qa.q: What did Harsha drag to the sink before dinner?
